result: The authors performed a complete 3D electron microscopy reconstruction of a 6 x 6 x 5 μm³ volume from hippocampal area CA1, identifying 449 synapses, 446 axons, and 149 dendrites across three animals. After exclusions for edge effects and shaft synapses, 287 valid spine synapses and 20 axon-coupled dendrite-coupled spine pairs were analyzed.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the study as 'elegant' and noted that 'the data were carefully and creatively analyzed.' They emphasized that 'the results are convincing because they have been reproduced in three animals (a very time consuming task).' No concerns were raised about the reconstruction methodology or sample identification.

result: The authors report strong correlations between spine head area and volume (r²=0.99), PSD area and spine head volume (r²=0.77), and other anatomical measurements. They found a weak trend between neck diameter and spine head volume but no correlation with neck length, consistent with previous studies. The distributions of these measurements are highly skewed with long tails.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question these correlational findings. The summary states that the study 'makes a simple but important point' and that results are 'convincing,' implicitly accepting these foundational anatomical correlations that underpin the main findings.

result: Axon-coupled spine pairs on the same dendrite had nearly identical head volumes (slope 0.91, CV=0.083, p=0.0002 vs random pairings). Strong correlations were also found for neck diameters, PSD areas, and docked vesicles. The precision was constant across all synapse sizes, with only a 1 in 5000 chance of random pairs being as precisely matched.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed this finding, stating 'the finding, that synapses that share an axon and a dendritic branch are very similar in size, is a very important confirmation of the notion that it is the history of correlated pre- and post-synaptic activity that determines synapse size and strength.' They noted 'high p values' as evidence of convincing results.

result: Spine neck lengths and neck volumes of axon-coupled pairs on the same dendrite were not well-correlated, indicating that regulation of neck length and neck volume are not important for synaptic strength.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this finding. The lack of correlation in neck measurements contrasts with the strong correlations in head volumes and other features, supporting the interpretation that neck dimensions are not tightly regulated for synaptic strength.

result: The near-identical size relationship observed for axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite does not hold for axon-coupled spines on different dendrites (CV=0.39, n=127) or for non-axon-coupled spines. These pairs were statistically indistinguishable from random pairings (KS test p=0.94) and showed no correlation in neck measurements.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as part of the overall pattern. Reviewer 1 noted 'It would be surprising if synapses made by the same axon on different dendrites of the same neuron...were not better correlated than synapses made onto different neurons,' suggesting the observed lack of correlation for different dendrites was expected and appropriate.

result: Spine head volumes ranged over a factor of 60 with a constant CV of 0.083 across all sizes. Using signal detection theory, the authors calculated that approximately 26 distinguishable synaptic strengths can span this range, corresponding to 4.7 bits of information storage per synapse. This represents non-uniform quantization that efficiently encodes the dynamic range at constant precision.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 requested that 'the rational and analysis should be described in the Results section in more detail which will make the data and the argument more understandable to a wider range of readers. Also a short discussion of how varying the discrimination threshold would affect the estimate would be useful.' This indicates the reviewers found the calculation and its presentation unclear, though they did not reject the approach.

result: The authors propose that time-window averaging over several minutes smooths out stochastic variability to achieve the observed precision (CV=0.083). They calculate averaging time windows ranging from 5.8 seconds to 21.8 minutes depending on release probability and spiking rate. Accounting for other sources of variability would require even longer time windows.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 stated 'I am not sure I quite follow the logic of the estimate for the time or the number of action potentials the paired synapses would need to average over to achieve the degree of similarity seen. During pre-synaptic bursts the release probability could go quite high, removing the noise due to the stochastic release seen during single APs.' This indicates confusion about the logic and potential issues with the calculation that were not fully resolved.

result: A total of 31,377 presynaptic vesicles were identified, with 3,437 labeled as docked (within 100 nm of the presynaptic membrane). These estimates were in good agreement with previous studies.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question the vesicle identification methodology or counts. The agreement with previous estimates and the careful methodology were implicitly accepted as part of the 'carefully and creatively analyzed' data.

result: The size difference of pairs of axon-coupled spines shows a weak trend with separation distance along the axon or dendrite.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 was 'puzzled by the statement "Difference in volume between pairs of spines is not correlated with separation distance"' and noted 'not observing a correlation does not imply that there isn't any' and 'it looks like there is a trend towards greater variability as the distance increases, which would indicate the involvement of a diffusible signal.' This suggests the reviewer saw evidence contradicting the authors' interpretation.

result: The sizes of axon-coupled spine pairs are unaffected by proximity of glial processes or location of mitochondria in the axon.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these negative findings. They are presented as control analyses showing that the observed precision is not explained by local anatomical factors.

result: The authors used Pearson's linear regression on log-normal transformed data for all analyses. The standard error of spine head volume measurements was less than 5% for most spines with a median error of about 1%. The coefficient of variation was calculated as the median of individual pair CVs, and distributions were compared using Kolmogorov-Smirnoff tests.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 raised a methodological concern: 'Ordering the spines by size before correlation analysis is inappropriate since it induces a correlation between them in the sense that knowing something about spine 1 tells me something about spine 2. Please randomize and redo the analysis.' This suggests a potential statistical artifact that could affect the results.

result: Previous studies underestimated precision by including spine neck volume. The authors excluded an unusual triple synapse from analysis but note this exclusion would not greatly affect the variability estimate.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question these methodological decisions. The exclusion of the triple synapse and the comparison to previous work were accepted as appropriate analytical choices.

result: Spine neck diameters were highly correlated between axon-coupled pairs (r²=0.70), despite the lack of correlation between spine head volumes and neck diameters in the population. This suggests at least two geometric aspects of spine geometry are under tight control of synaptic plasticity, possibly reflecting different functional aspects such as material trafficking.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this unexpected finding. It is presented as a novel observation about the regulation of spine geometry that extends beyond the main finding about head volumes.

result: The authors cite complementary findings from neocortex and mouse cortex showing similar precision in synaptic plasticity, suggesting the phenomenon may be general across brain areas. They note that synaptic tagging and capture is less effective across different dendritic branches.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question these contextualizing citations. They are presented as supporting evidence that the findings may generalize beyond hippocampus.

result: The authors propose that CaMKII phosphorylation, which integrates calcium signals over minutes to hours, provides a biochemical mechanism for the observed time-window averaging. The time windows for CaMKII integration match those predicted by the model and are similar to those in synaptic tagging and capture.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this mechanistic proposal. It is presented as a plausible biochemical explanation for the observed precision, though it remains speculative.

result: The authors propose that stochastic variability in synaptic transmission may reflect an energy-efficient sampling strategy where each synapse samples from a probability distribution with a highly accurate mean. This could function like 'drop out' regularization in machine learning, reducing overfitting.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these speculative computational interpretations. They are presented as potential functional explanations for why high precision in the physical substrate coexists with stochastic transmission.

result: The authors acknowledge that the upper bound on variability may be limited by reconstruction errors and could be even lower with more accurate methods.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question this limitation. It is presented as an appropriate acknowledgment of methodological constraints.
